title: Context & Long-Range Notes: Deep-dive + ICLR takeaways
content:
Purpose: scratchpad for ideas from ICLR session (Aug 2026) + follow-up reading. Goal = pick 2 experiments we can ship in a week: (1) lightweight KV eviction probe across seq lengths, (2) cheap prefix cache that preserves early-turn coherence.

Top-line takeaways ICLR '26 sessions & papers I skimmed
- Sparse kernel attention variants (paper A): good speedups for mid-length (1k-4k) but not great at >8k. Their multi-block scheduling idea seems promising for batching tradeoffs; could combine with our kernel selector to pick schedule per model/seq-distribution.
- Latent-index retrieval (paper B): compress contexts into small latent vectors and retrieve by similarity to hidden states. Very cheap for cold-starts, might help when full KV cache misses for long conversations.
- KV sharding + MoE routing (paper C): dynamic routing of keys to shard targets reduces memory by ~25% but increases tail latency unless routing is amortized. Worth prototyping under dedicated to measure real tail impact.

Notes-to-self / immediate questions
- How brittle are sparse kernels across model families? Paper A tested on LLaMA-style architectures; our tested catalog includes Mixtral & Mistral variants. Need quick bench on Mistral-7B.
- For latent-index retrieval: what is staleness window? is it okay for convo contexts where user edits prior turns?
- Eviction heuristics: oldest-token vs least-recently-used vs prediction-based keepers (e.g., tokens that influence gradient-attention weights). Could we cheaply approximate "importance" using last-layer attention norm?

Short summaries (for later PRD blurbs)
- Paper A (sparse-kernel-attention): batching-friendly kernels that slice sequence into overlapping blocks; pro: CPU-friendly for many short requests; con: loses accuracy at extreme lengths and introduces boundary artifacts. Implementation note: need a small transformer-compatible shim to align block boundaries with positional embeddings.
- Paper B (latent-context-index): encoder maps chunks -> 64-d latents; retrieval by dot-product; authors show 10x reduction in memory for context retrieval but +2-6% accuracy drop on long-form QA. Good candidate for experimental fallback path on cache miss.
- Paper C (kv-moeroute): MoE-style routers assigned to KV slices. Interesting for horizontal memory scaling; needs routing warmup to avoid cold-miss spikes.

Experiment ideas (priority order)
1) Eviction-probe (3 days): implement a tiny harness that simulates KV population from convo logs (use 5k convo snippets). Compare eviction heuristics on intrinsic metric: fraction of tokens in top-10 attention for next N tokens. Output: ROC-like curve for heuristics.
2) Latent-fallback path (week): build a small encoder (distil-BERT-ish) that maps 512-token chunks -> 64-d vectors. On KV miss, query latent-index top-k and reconstruct partial KV. Measure generation perplexity and latency delta.
3) Kernel-selector tweak (2-3 days): add paper-A's schedule option into our kernel selection table. Run small microbench on Mistral-7B to see perf delta for 512/2k/8k.
4) Dedicated pilot: KV-shard routing stress test (needs SRE signoff). Warmup routing with synthetic traffic and measure p99 latency.

Data / infra notes
- Use archived convo corpus: /mnt/data/research/convos/2026-q2 (sanitized).
- Small harness repo: github.com/redwood-inference/ctx-probes (create feature/evict-probe branch). Add synthetic generator that simulates edit events (user edits earlier turns) for staleness tests.
- Metrics: token-hit-rate, next-token perplexity delta, p50/p95/p99 latency for retrieval path, CPU/GPU memory footprint.

Open design tradeoffs (write for sync session with Ravi)
- Accuracy vs memory: latent retrieval shrinks memory but may drop fidelity. Which workloads can tolerate ~5% drop? support-bot vs creative writing?
- Complexity vs maintainability: kernel schedule layer increases code paths in serving runtime. Is this acceptable for hosted API? maybe limit to Dedicated for now.
- Observability: need synthetic canaries that specifically validate early-turn coherence after eviction. Put these into Optimize dashboard as "context-regression-tests".

To-dos (concrete)
- [ ] Kickoff quick bench: microkernel tests on Mistral-7B (assigned: Mika) — due 2026-08-24
- [ ] Spin up evict-probe harness and run on sample convo set (assigned: me) — due 2026-08-26
- [ ] Draft simple latent-encoder (poc) and run retrieval quality (assigned: Ravi + Elyse) — scope 7 days
- [ ] Post findings to #research-long-context with short scoreboard (p99, hit-rate, perp-delta)

Useful links / bookmarks (copied from session)
- "Efficient Sparse Kernels for Attention" — https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01234
- "Latent Indexes for Long Context" — https://acme.ai/papers/latent-index-2026
- Internal ticket: github.com/redwood-inference/mosaic-cache/issues/42
- Slack thread: #long-context-questions (https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C01234ABC)

Quick sketch of eviction-probe harness (notes)
- Input: tokenized convo stream, build per-turn KV references (simulate positions).
- For each eviction policy: simulate building cache up to size S, then measure how often the next-turn's top-attended tokens are present.
- Heuristic to rank token "importance": alpha * attention_norm + beta * recency. Sweep alpha/beta.
- Output: CSV with (policy, cache_size, hit_rate, avg_importance_of_evicted).

Unresolved / nice-to-have
- Can we instrument model to cheaply surface attention-norm per token during generation without huge perf hit? If yes, that unlocks prediction-based eviction cheaply.
- If latent fallback is viable, how to stitch tokens back into KV so that subsequent queries use them naturally (positional offsets, mixing with real KV)?

Notes-to-self: keep the doc lightweight, move polished notes to Confluence only after we have hard numbers. This doc = workbench + meeting prep for 2026-09-03 sync with Platform and Dedicated teams.

End of scratchpad.
